title: Made-Up Answers
about: Why chatbots sometimes invent facts, and how to catch them.

cards.prompt: This model only read space stories like "Captain Rivera stepped onto Mars". What's it **most likely** to write next?
cards.context: The first person to walk on Mars was
cards.hint: It isn't choosing what's true. What did this model read again and again?
cards.nudge: Think about its stories. Which word filled this spot in them?
cards.explanation: Nobody has walked on Mars yet (Neil Armstrong walked on the **Moon**), but in its stories this line goes on "**Captain** …". So it invents a Mars walker, one likely word at a time.

cards.title: Fluent, confident, wrong
cards.body: A **hallucination** is when a chatbot says something false, smoothly and confidently. It picks words that *sound* likely, not checked facts, so a made-up book sounds as real as a true one. Watch names, dates, numbers, quotes and sources: check them in a trusted source, like a library catalogue. Asking "are you sure?" checks nothing.

cards.prompt: You're writing a report on volcanoes.

steps.text: A chatbot suggests the book "Fire Below" by Dr Helen Marsh, with a quote for your report. What do you do?

choices.text: Use the quote: the chatbot named the book
choices.consequence: Nobody can find the book: it doesn't exist. A made-up quote in a report is a real problem.

choices.text: Search for the book in the library catalogue
choices.consequence: No results for the book or the author. None of it exists.

choices.text: Ask the chatbot whether the book is real
choices.consequence: It says "Yes, it's a well-known book!" It can be just as sure about a hallucination.

steps.text: The library has never heard of it. What now?

choices.text: Leave it out, and find a real source in the library
choices.consequence: Right: the book was a hallucination. A real source gives you facts you can trust.

choices.text: Keep the quote, but don't say where it's from
choices.consequence: The quote is made up too, and now it's hidden. Use a real source.

cards.hint: What's a trusted source for whether a book exists?
cards.explanation: Titles, authors and quotes are classic hallucinations: **check them in a trusted source**, like a library catalogue. Asking the chatbot doesn't help.

cards.prompt: **Double-check** each chatbot answer, or **fine as it is**? Health questions go to a doctor, pharmacist or trusted adult.

items.label: A date for a history project
A quote from a famous scientist
A website it says it got facts from
Names for a new team group chat

cards.hint: Ask: if it were made up, would it matter?
cards.nudge: Ideas can't really be wrong; facts, quotes, sources and health can, and it matters.
cards.explanation: Dates, quotes, sources and health facts could be hallucinated, so double-check (medicine: a doctor, pharmacist or trusted adult). Themes, rhymes and chat names have no "wrong" to catch.

cards.prompt: A chatbot gives you a fact for a work report. What's the **best** way to check it?

options.text: Find it in a trusted source, like an official website
Ask the same question again and compare answers
options.nudge: A chatbot can repeat a mistake. Where can you check outside it?

options.text: Ask the chatbot how it knows, and if it's sure
options.nudge: It can be confidently wrong about its own mistakes. Where else could you look?

options.text: Ask a different chatbot if it gives the same answer
options.nudge: Another chatbot can make the same mistake. Where can you check outside chatbots?

cards.hint: The check has to come from somewhere that isn't a chatbot.
cards.explanation: Only a **trusted source** outside chatbots really checks a fact. Asking again, asking how it knows or asking another chatbot can repeat or defend a hallucination.

cards.prompt: A chatbot says a famous ship sank in **1915**, with a link to a museum website.

steps.text: The link opens a real museum page about the ship. What now?

choices.text: Use 1915: the link works, so it's checked
choices.consequence: The page is real, but it says **1912**. A real link isn't proof of the claim.

choices.text: Read the page and find the date it gives
Ask the chatbot to double-check its date
choices.consequence: It apologises and says 1914. The answer is on the page you already have.

steps.text: The page says 1912; the chatbot said 1915. Which do you use?

choices.text: 1912: what the museum page actually says
choices.consequence: Right: the trusted source you actually read wins.

choices.text: 1915: the chatbot found the page, so it knows
choices.consequence: It linked the right page but wrote the wrong date. Go with the source.

cards.hint: A source only checks a fact if it really says what the chatbot claims.
cards.explanation: A working link isn't enough: chatbots can link a real page and still get details wrong. **Read the source** and go with what it says.

cards.prompt: Match each thing a chatbot gives you to what to do about it.

pairs.left: Says where a fact came from
pairs.right: Open the source and read it

cards.hint: Is each one a fact to check, a source to open, a health question, or just ideas?
cards.nudge: Ideas can't be wrong and health needs an expert. Which is the book, which the source?
cards.explanation: Books: check a **catalogue**. Sources: **open and read** them. Medicine: ask a **doctor or pharmacist**. Party themes are ideas, so there's nothing to catch.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **hallucination** is a confident, false answer built from likely words.
- They hide in names, dates, numbers, quotes and sources.
- Check what matters in a trusted source, not by asking again.

Next: the module quiz.
